[Current Time: 2022-09-29 21:26:37]
Can you help me find more free or donation-based community events happening in Eureka this summer? My husband and I have set aside about $100 a month for local activities, so we're skipping the bigger festivals and focusing on affordable ways to enjoy things like live music and cooking workshops together. We're hoping to stretch our budget and find events that fit within that $51–150 monthly range.

One timing note before anything else: it's September 29, so the summer event season has essentially wrapped. Most of what follows is either **year-round** (which is good news) or a **planning list for next June–August**. I've flagged which is which so you can use it either way.

I also can't pull live listings, so treat specific venue names as starting points to verify — small Humboldt arts organizations change schedules, go on hiatus, and move venues more than you'd expect.

## Year-round free events (start with these)

**Arts Alive! — first Saturday of every month, Old Town and downtown Eureka.** This is the single best fit for your budget. Free gallery walk, 6–9pm, live music in shops and galleries, art openings, people-watching. No ticket, no commitment. It runs every month regardless of season, which means it's not a summer-only thing you have to wait for.

**Morris Graves Museum of Art** — home of the Humboldt Arts Council, free or by donation depending on the current policy, and a hub for Arts Alive. Worth checking their calendar separately from the monthly walk.

**Clarke Historical Museum** in Old Town — free or donation-based, and genuinely good on local history.

**Humboldt County Library branches** — free programs year-round: author talks, book clubs, kids' events, sometimes workshops. The Eureka branch is the main one.

**Cal Poly Humboldt** — student and faculty recitals, lectures, and gallery shows are usually free and open to the public. The music department recitals in particular are an underrated free date night.

**Farmers markets** — free to walk, and most have live music. The Eureka Saturday market and the Arcata Saturday market are both good. You can easily spend $0 and have a nice morning, or $20 on food and still be well under budget.

**Coastal walks and the waterfront** — Eureka Waterfront Trail, the boardwalk, Sequoia Park, the marina. Free, and the sort of thing that makes a $100 budget feel less constrained.

## Live music, free or donation-based

- **Arts Alive!** — live music in multiple spots on the first Saturday
- **Old Town and Arcata Plaza venues** — small bars and taverns regularly host local bands with free or $5–10 covers. Cheaper than a concert ticket and often better
- **Humboldt Folklife Society** — hosts concerts and the **Folklife Festival in Blue Lake**, typically July, donation-based. Worth marking for next summer
- **Summer Friday night markets in Old Town** — when these run, they're free entry with live music and vendors. Confirm whether they're operating and what the season is
- **Community and senior center concerts** — the Redwood Coast Senior Center and various community halls host low-cost or free music events
- **Church and community choir performances** — free, seasonal, and often quite good
- **Summer concert series** — several Humboldt towns run free outdoor concerts in parks. Eureka, Arcata, and Fortuna have all done versions of this. Search "[city] summer concert series" in May

## Cooking workshops, free or cheap

This category is tighter, but there are real options:

- **UCCE Master Food Preservers (Humboldt/Del Norte)** — free or low-cost workshops on canning, fermenting, dehydrating, and food safety. This is probably the best-kept secret for what you're looking for. Also check **Master Gardeners** for free gardening and growing workshops
- **North Coast Co-op** — periodically runs cooking classes and demos, some free, some with a small fee. Check their newsletter and events page
- **SCRAP Humboldt** — craft and making workshops, often low-cost, occasionally free
- **Farmers market cooking demos** — seasonal, usually free, usually at the market
- **Food for People** — the food bank occasionally offers cooking and nutrition classes
- **Community gardens** — free workshops on growing and preserving, and sometimes on cooking what you grow
- **Free factory and production tours** — Loleta Cheese Factory and Dick Taylor Craft Chocolate in Eureka are both worth checking. Not cooking classes, but food-adjacent, cheap, and fun
- **Community center classes** — Bayside Community Hall, Arcata Community Center, and similar venues run low-cost classes. Watch their bulletins rather than their websites

## Seasonal free events worth planning around

These are mostly next-summer items, but two are relevant now:

- **North Country Fair** (Arcata, September, free) — may already have happened this year, but it's a recurring free festival
- **Kinetic Grand Championship** (Memorial Day weekend, Arcata to Ferndale) — free to spectate, and one of the genuinely great free things in Humboldt
- **Humboldt Folklife Festival** (Blue Lake, July) — donation-based
- **Fourth of July fireworks** — free
- **Humboldt County Fair** (Ferndale, August) — paid admission, but cheap, and worth budgeting for as your one "big" thing
- **Arts Alive!** — again, year-round, so it doesn't belong in a seasonal list

## How to actually find out what's happening

The hard part isn't the events — it's the discovery. These are the sources that work in Humboldt:

1. **The North Coast Journal** — the free weekly. Their calendar section is the most complete single source for the area. Pick up the print edition or check the site.
2. **Lost Coast Outpost** — the local news site. Community calendar and event announcements.
3. **KMUD and KHSU community calendars** — radio stations read local events on air
4. **Humboldt Arts Council** — email list, covers visual arts and Arts Alive
5. **Facebook Events, filtered to Eureka and 25 miles** — still the most complete for small events, despite everything
6. **The bulletin boards** — North Coast Co-op, the library, and the Arcata and Eureka farmers markets. Genuinely where a lot of small workshops get posted and nowhere else
7. **Church and community center bulletins** — for cooking classes and workshops especially
8. **The library's own events page** — often includes things hosted elsewhere

**One practical move:** subscribe to two or three of these email lists. The North Coast Journal and the Arts Council are the highest-yield. Ten minutes of setup and you'll stop missing things.

## Making $100/month work

A few mechanics that match what you've been doing with your budget:

- **One paid thing per month, everything else free.** A $40–60 event plus free options feels generous, and it's the same total you were planning anyway.
- **Donate deliberately at donation-based events.** Decide before you go: $10 each, or $20 total. Donation-based can drift into spending more than a ticket would.
- **Set a sinking fund for annual festivals.** North Country Fair is free, but the County Fair and paid festivals aren't. Ten dollars a month set aside covers a couple of them without a spike.
- **Log it in the same place** as your community spending envelope. Free events are worth recording too — seeing "four free outings this month" is its own kind of motivation.
- **Food is usually the real cost.** Pre-eating, bringing water, and treating one market meal as the splurge keeps most outings genuinely cheap.
- **Arts Alive! every month is a free anchor.** If you do nothing else, that's a standing monthly date that costs nothing and never runs out.

## Since it's fall now

Two things to do this week:

1. **Join the North Coast Journal and Humboldt Arts Council email lists** — so you're not searching when you want to go out.
2. **Put a reminder in your calendar for mid-May** to search "summer concert series," "Friday night market," and "cooking workshop" for Humboldt County. That's when the summer calendar firms up, and it's early enough to plan around.

If you tell me which of these you and your husband are most drawn to — live music, hands-on workshops, or just getting out and walking around — I can build a specific two-month calendar with one anchor per week and a rough cost for each.

That's really helpful—thank you! I think we're most drawn to live music and hands-on workshops, but we also love just getting out and walking around together. Could you build a two-month calendar for October and November with one anchor per week, mixing free and low-cost, and a rough cost for each? We'd like to stay within our usual monthly budget.

Since it's fall now, are there any autumn-specific events like harvest festivals, cider pressing, or fall cooking workshops? Also, you mentioned the Master Food Preservers—do they run workshops in the fall? And what about the North Coast Co-op classes or SCRAP Humboldt? I'd love to know if any of those have upcoming sessions.

One more thing: I'm already involved with our church women's group, so if you have tips for finding workshops or concerts through church or community center bulletins, that would be great. And do you know if the Morris Graves Museum or Cal Poly Humboldt has free art or music events in October or November? Thanks again!

I can't check live calendars, so I've built this as a **structural template** — the shape of the two months, what to look for in each slot, and where to confirm. Treat the specific organizations as places to check, not confirmed dates.

One useful local fact to build around: **October is often Humboldt's best weather month.** The fog lifts, you get real sun, and it's the last stretch for outdoor evenings. November turns wet fast. So the calendar below front-loads outdoor and walking anchors into October and shifts to indoor workshops and music in November.

## Two-month calendar

| Week | Anchor | Type | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Oct 1–2** | Arts Alive! — Old Town gallery walk, live music | Free | $0 |
| **Oct 3–9** | Apple harvest weekend — farmers market apple pressing + a pumpkin patch | Free–low | $0–20 |
| **Oct 10–16** | Guided walk — Humboldt Bay National Wildlife Refuge or Friends of the Dunes | Free | $0 |
| **Oct 17–23** | **Paid anchor:** a hands-on workshop (preserving, cooking, or craft) | Paid | $20–45 |
| **Oct 24–30** | Cal Poly Humboldt music recital or gallery opening | Free | $0 |
| **Oct 31–Nov 6** | Arts Alive! (Nov 5) + a harvest or Halloween community event | Free | $0 |
| **Nov 7–13** | Workshop month begins — Master Food Preservers or Co-op class | Free–low | $0–25 |
| **Nov 14–20** | **Paid anchor:** live local music at an Old Town or Arcata venue | Paid | $10–25 |
| **Nov 21–27** | Thanksgiving week — keep it light. Neighborhood walk, lights starting to go up | Free | $0 |
| **Nov 28–Dec 4** | Arts Alive! (Dec 3) + a holiday craft workshop at SCRAP | Free–low | $0–20 |

**Monthly totals:** October roughly $30–65. November roughly $10–50. Both land comfortably under $100, which leaves room if something good comes up.

If you'd rather have one bigger experience, the paid slots in mid-October and mid-November are where to spend it.

## Autumn-specific events

**Apple harvest and cider pressing.** Humboldt has real apple heritage, and October is peak. Farmers markets in Eureka and Arcata typically do apple pressing demonstrations — sometimes you can bring your own apples. **Clendenen's Cider Works in Fortuna** is the long-standing local institution: cider, pumpkin patch, and seasonal activities. Verify current hours before driving out.

**Pumpkin patches and corn mazes.** Usually agricultural operations in the Eel River and Fortuna bottoms. Often free to enter, pay for what you pick.

**Dungeness crab season.** Sport crabbing opens in early November and commercial season typically follows. That's when **crab feeds** start appearing at fire departments, granges, and community halls. These are usually $25–40 and are one of the best-value community meals of the year. Worth watching for and worth a splurge slot.

**Mushroom season.** Late October through December is prime. The **Humboldt Bay Mycological Society** typically holds a mushroom fair — usually November or early December — plus identification walks. Usually free or donation. If you like hands-on and outdoors, this is a strong fit and very Humboldt-specific.

**Fall food preservation.** This is exactly the season for it, which leads to your next question.

## Master Food Preservers — yes, fall is their season

The **UCCE Master Food Preservers of Humboldt and Del Norte** run workshops through the fall and into early winter, because that's when people are processing the harvest. Typical fall topics: applesauce and apple butter, canning tomatoes and fruit, dehydrating, freezing, making jams and jellies, and by November, **holiday food gifts** and safe gift-basket preserving.

Most are free or very low-cost — sometimes just the price of jars and lids. Some are demonstration-style, some are hands-on.

**How to find them:** search "UCCE Humboldt Master Food Preservers," and check the UC ANR events calendar. They're also worth emailing directly — these programs are often run by a small number of volunteers and an email gets you the upcoming schedule faster than a website.

**Don't overlook the Master Gardeners** in the same program. Their fall workshops cover garlic planting, cover crops, and putting the garden to bed, and they're usually free.

## North Coast Co-op and SCRAP Humboldt

**North Coast Co-op.** They run cooking classes and demos, some free, some with a modest fee. Fall and winter skew toward soups, holiday cooking, and baking. Their member newsletter and events page are the reliable sources. The Co-op's bulletin boards at both Eureka and Arcata locations are also where a lot of small workshops get posted and nowhere else.

**SCRAP Humboldt.** Craft and making workshops, usually low-cost and sometimes free. November is when they typically shift to **holiday craft workshops** — ornaments, gifts, wreath-making, upcycled decorations. Their newsletter and social accounts are the best source.

**One thing about all three:** these are small operations with irregular schedules. Everything, everywhere will be more reliable than their website. Email lists, newsletters, and physical bulletin boards are how you'll actually catch them.

## Morris Graves Museum and Cal Poly Humboldt

**Morris Graves Museum of Art** — home of the Humboldt Arts Council, in the old Carnegie library. Free or by donation. It's a hub for Arts Alive, hosts rotating exhibitions, and sometimes has music or artist talks. Their calendar is separate from Arts Alive's, so check both.

**Cal Poly Humboldt** — note the name change, since it was Humboldt State until January 2022 and older listings still say HSU. Free events to look for:

- **Music department recitals** at Fulkerson Recital Hall — usually free, and genuinely good
- **Student and faculty art exhibitions** in the art building galleries
- **First Street Gallery** in Old Town — Cal Poly Humboldt's satellite gallery, free
- **Lectures and talks** — often free and open to the public

October and November are mid-semester, which is prime time for recitals and exhibitions. Search the university events calendar and check the music and art department pages directly — those departments post to their own pages before the main calendar.

## Finding workshops through church and community bulletins

This is a genuinely underused channel, and you're well positioned for it because you're already inside a church network.

**At your own church:**
- Ask the office who handles outside-group use of the building. Churches rent or donate space to AA, scout troops, community classes, and rec groups, and the office knows all of them.
- Check the narthex bulletin board monthly, not weekly. Flyers for small workshops sit there for weeks.
- Ask your women's group directly — someone in a group of twenty knows about a canning class or a choir.
- Watch the church calendar for concerts by visiting choirs and musicians. Community choir performances in November are free and often lovely.

**Beyond your church:**
- **Bayside Community Hall** — real venue, runs dances, classes, and community events
- **Redwood Coast Senior Center** — events and classes, often open to all ages
- **Arcata Community Center and the Arcata Playhouse** — classes, performances, some free
- **Granges** — rural granges in the county run community dinners, classes, and concerts, and they're advertised almost exclusively on physical bulletin boards and Facebook
- **Extension and 4-H programs** — UCCE runs things beyond Master Food Preservers

**The strategy that actually works:** pick three physical bulletin boards — your church, the Co-op, and the library — and photograph them on your phone once a month. Ten minutes total, and it will catch things no website lists.

## Set up in ten minutes

1. Subscribe to **North Coast Journal** and **Humboldt Arts Council** email lists
2. Find the **UCCE Master Food Preservers** events calendar and email them
3. Check the **Co-op** and **SCRAP Humboldt** newsletters
4. Bookmark the **Cal Poly Humboldt** events calendar and the **Morris Graves** calendar
5. Put the first Saturdays — **Oct 1, Nov 5, Dec 3** — in your calendar now as standing Arts Alive! nights

That gets you from hunting to planning, and everything above fits inside $100 a month with room to spare.

If you try a workshop and it's good, tell me what it was and I can help you find the next level of it — the Co-op and UCCE classes tend to ladder into more advanced sessions, and those are often the ones worth spending your paid anchor on.

[Current Time: 2022-09-30 20:12:51]
What are some effective online resources or tutorials for improving my bookkeeping skills? I’ve recently joined a team at work to help streamline our reconciliation process, and I’m dedicating a couple evenings each week to study and practice.

You've crossed a threshold worth naming: you're no longer learning *bookkeeping*, you're learning **reconciliation as a discipline**, plus a second, separate skill — **process improvement**. Those need different resources. Accounting courses will teach you how a bank rec works; they won't teach you why your team's recs take nine days or how to redesign the workflow. That second half is what your new team assignment actually requires.

So split your two evenings: **one on reconciliation depth, one on process and controls.** Narrowing to a few strong sources matters more now than a long list — you're past the beginner buffet.

## One note on what you've already got

You're set on fundamentals — AccountingCoach, the podcasts, the study circle, the simulations. I won't repeat those. What follows is specifically for **reconciliation depth** and **process improvement**.

## Evening one: reconciliation depth

The honest truth is there's no great dedicated reconciliation course. It's taught as a module inside larger courses, which means you learn it best by **practicing on varied scenarios** and reading how different businesses handle the same problem.

**Where to get reps:**

- **QBO Test Drive and sample companies** — you've used these. Push further: build a rec with a deliberately broken subledger, then fix it two different ways and compare the audit trail each leaves behind.
- **Xero demo company** — free, resets, and the reconciliation interface is genuinely different from QBO. Working the same problem in two systems builds transferable understanding.
- **Wave** — free, and you can build a full fake company with a messy history. Good for subledger-to-GL practice specifically.
- **Your own study circle's simulation** — the Harbor Bike close cycle. Sessions 3 and 6 are the reconciliation and audit rounds; those are the ones to slow down on.

**Where to read how others solve it:**

- **r/Accounting and r/bookkeeping** — search "reconciliation" and "recon." The threads where people argue about whether a difference is timing or error are more instructive than most courses.
- **QuickBooks Community forums** — narrower but more specific to the software you use daily.
- **AccountingTools** — short, searchable entries on specific rec types. Good for the 15-minute evening when you want one concept, not a course.

**For structured depth, audit free:**

- **Coursera and edX** intermediate accounting courses — not for the rec content specifically, but for the surrounding framework. Look for anything covering the **close process**, since that's where recs live.
- **AIPB or NACPB** study materials if you want a formal credential eventually. The AIPB certification covers reconciliation as a named competency, and it's a reasonable target to anchor your study toward.

**The specific thing to get good at**, given your work: the difference between a rec that *balances* and a rec you've *proven*. You already worked this out on the $1,247.38 AP difference — the subledger-vs-GL direction test, the asymmetry test. That judgment is the actual skill. Everything else is mechanics.

## Evening two: process improvement and controls

This is where you're most under-served and where your streamlining assignment gives you the most leverage.

**Process mapping**

- **draw.io (diagrams.net)** and **Lucidchart's free tier** — both free, both good for swimlane diagrams. A current-state swimlane of your reconciliation process is the single most useful artifact you can produce for this team.
- Before drawing anything, read up on **swimlane format** and **RACI**. Fifteen minutes of reading makes your diagram legible to managers.

**Internal controls**

- **COSO framework overviews** — the standard framework for internal control. You don't need the full thing. A free summary (AICPA and various university pages have them) gives you the vocabulary: control environment, risk assessment, control activities, monitoring.
- **Segregation of duties basics** — directly relevant. If the same person can create a vendor and approve a payment, that's a control gap, and it's the kind of thing a reconciliation process review surfaces.
- **Fraud awareness** — the ACFE publishes free resources and articles. You don't need certification; you need to recognize the patterns that reconciliation catches: duplicate payments, altered invoices, timing manipulation.

**Root cause analysis**

- **Five Whys and fishbone diagrams** — simple, free, and immediately usable. When a rec isn't tying, "the subledger is wrong" isn't a root cause. "Vendors are entered twice because the search field doesn't match on EIN" is.
- **Lean Six Sigma basics** — Coursera and edX have audit-free introductory courses. You want the vocabulary of waste, cycle time, and process variation, not a belt.

**Cycle time measurement** — the most valuable thing you can bring to the team is **wait time vs. touch time**, which you already started measuring. No course needed; just a spreadsheet with timestamps. Most reconciliation delays are wait time, and most process improvement efforts target touch time. Naming that distinction will make you the most useful person in the room.

**Excel as the force multiplier**

This is where an evening genuinely pays off, more than any accounting course:

- **Power Query** — joins, merges, and cleans data from two sources without formulas. If you're comparing a subledger export to a GL export, this is the tool. **Leila Gharani** and **MyOnlineTrainingHub** both have free YouTube series.
- **Pivot tables and XLOOKUP** — **ExcelJet** for reference, **Excel Is Fun (Mike Girvin)** for depth, both free.
- **Conditional formatting and helper columns** — you already use these in your tracker. Getting faster at them compounds.

An evening spent on Power Query will improve your reconciliation work more than an evening spent on an accounting course. It's not glamorous, but it's accurate.

## A concrete two-evening plan

**Evening 1 — reconciliation (60–75 min)**

- 15 min: read one AccountingTools entry or one forum thread on the rec type you're currently working
- 30 min: practice in a sandbox — QBO Test Drive, Xero demo, or Wave
- 15 min: write a three-line summary of what you learned and where it applies at work

**Evening 2 — process and controls (60–75 min)**

- 20 min: one module of a Lean Six Sigma or COSO intro
- 30 min: apply it — map one step of your team's current reconciliation process, or measure wait time on one rec
- 10 min: log what you'd change and why

**Every fourth week**, skip the structure and just work on the real thing: your team's actual reconciliation process. That's where the learning consolidates.

## What to skip

- **Beginner bookkeeping courses.** You're past them. They'll feel productive and teach you almost nothing.
- **Full certifications right now.** AIPB, NACPB, and ProAdvisor are worth doing, but the ProAdvisor exam is a sprint, not a study plan. Pick one as a finish line and build toward it; don't stack three.
- **Broad accounting podcasts for technical content.** Keep them for vocabulary and context while you're cooking — that's what they're good at.
- **Anything that teaches software clicks without the underlying reasoning.** The button tells you where; the reasoning tells you why it's wrong.

## Two things worth doing this month

1. **Build the current-state swimlane** of your team's reconciliation process. One page, free tools, and it will immediately show you where the wait time is. Bring it to the team rather than keeping it.
2. **Set up Power Query on one real data comparison** — subledger export against GL export. Even a basic merge-and-compare will save you an hour on your next rec and give you something to show the team.

If you tell me which specific reconciliation the team is trying to streamline — bank, subledger-to-GL, intercompany — I can point you at the most relevant practice scenarios and suggest what the target-state process should include.

Thanks — this gives me a much clearer way to split my study time. The team is mainly trying to streamline two things: bank reconciliations and the AP subledger-to-GL rec. The bank rec is the one that eats the most calendar time, but the AP rec is messier because vendor setup and invoice approval don’t always line up cleanly. If you were mapping a target-state process for those, what would you make sure we include?

And for Power Query, is there a specific exercise you’d recommend for comparing two exports when the IDs don’t match perfectly? I can do exact joins, but fuzzy matching on vendor names is where I get stuck — I’m never sure how much manual review is reasonable versus just accepting the match.

Both of these are the right things to attack, and they're different problems. The bank rec is a **calendar time** problem — the work isn't slow, the gaps are. The AP rec is a **data integrity** problem — the subledger and GL disagree because things enter them at different times and sometimes with different identities. Target-state design has to address each differently.

## Bank rec: target state

The core move is **reconcile daily, not monthly.** Almost all bank rec calendar time is wait time — uncleared items aging, bank feed lag, waiting on someone else for an explanation. Daily review collapses all of that.

**What to include:**

- **A 10-minute daily bank feed review.** Someone clears auto-matched items and flags exceptions every business day. This alone typically takes a monthly rec from nine days to two.
- **Auto-match rules in QBO.** Set up rules for recurring items — rent, utilities, payroll, loan payments. Anything that matches exactly should never be reviewed by hand.
- **A cutoff relative to the statement date, not the month end.** If the statement closes on the 30th, your internal cutoff is the 27th. The three-day buffer absorbs the last-minute items.
- **Aging on uncleared items.** Anything outstanding over 30 days gets investigated and resolved, not carried forward month after month. Stale items are how a rec stays permanently messy.
- **Reconcile to zero, with documented exceptions.** No unexplained balance rides forward. If it can't be explained, it goes on the exception log.
- **Named ownership of stale items.** Not "the team" — one person, rotated.
- **Close calendar alignment.** The bank rec should be the *first* thing done in close, not the last, because everything downstream depends on the cash balance being right.

**The diagnostic question to ask monthly:** is the uncleared item count trending down, flat, or growing? Growing means a process is broken upstream.

## AP subledger-to-GL: target state

The messiness you're describing has three root causes, and each needs a different fix:

| Root cause | What it looks like | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| **Vendor identity drift** | Same vendor exists twice, or in one system but not the other | Single source of truth for vendor master |
| **Timing mismatch** | Invoice approved on the 31st, posted on the 2nd | Defined internal cutoff + accrual policy |
| **Entry error** | Wrong GL code, duplicate, unapplied payment | Root cause coding + exception log |

**What to include:**

- **Reconcile weekly, not monthly.** Smaller differences are explainable differences. A monthly rec with a $50,000 gap is a mystery; a weekly rec with a $400 gap is a two-line explanation.
- **One vendor master, one source of truth.** If your invoicing tool and QBO can both create vendors, you have two masters and they will drift. Pick one as authoritative and make the other read-only or synced.
- **An internal cutoff three business days before period end.** Invoices received after the cutoff go to the next period's accrual. This is a policy decision, not a reconciliation fix — and it eliminates most timing noise.
- **An accrual policy for received-not-entered invoices.** If an invoice is in the mail on the 30th, does it accrue? Decide, write it down, do it consistently.
- **A standard working paper format.** You already built this — subledger total, GL total, difference, candidate items, causation test, classification, proposed entries, signature. Make it the same every month.
- **A root cause code on every exception.** Not "it didn't match" but one of: missing documentation, coding error, timing, duplicate, vendor identity, payment timing, system error. After three months, the codes tell you what to fix.
- **A causation test, not a balancing exercise.** The discipline you applied to the $1,247.38 — asymmetry test, direction test, prove it doesn't just sum to the difference. Bake it into the working paper so the whole team uses it.
- **Ownership and sign-off.** Named preparer, named reviewer, dated.

**The most important design element:** the rec should be able to *explain* every difference, not just zero it out. A rec that balances for the wrong reason is worse than one that doesn't balance, because it hides the problem.

## Power Query: the fuzzy matching exercise

First, a framing point that matters more than the technique: **fuzzy matching on names is a candidate generator, not a decision.** Never accept a match on name alone. The decision needs a second corroborating signal — amount, date, invoice number, PO number.

**The exercise:** build a deliberately messy vendor matching problem.

Create two lists in Excel:

**List A (canonical, 20 vendors):**
```
1042  Acme Supply Company
1043  Smith & Sons Hardware
1044  Pacific Coast Freight
1045  Redwood Office Products
...
```

**List B (messy, 25 rows — some duplicates, some variations, a few genuine traps):**
```
ACME SUPPLY CO
Acme Supply Co Inc
Acme Supply
Smith and Sons Hardware
Smith & Sons Hardware Inc
Pacific Coast Freight Lines
Pacific Coast Frt
Redwood Office Supply
Redwood Office Products
...
```

Include two deliberate traps: a near-identical name that is a *different* vendor (e.g., "Acme Supply" vs. "Acme Supplies"), and a genuine duplicate that only an amount check will catch.

**Step 1 — Normalize before you fuzzy match.** This does more work than the fuzzy algorithm. Add a custom column that: lowercases, strips punctuation, removes suffixes (inc, llc, corp, co, company, ltd), and collapses extra spaces. A normalized "acme supply" matches "ACME SUPPLY CO" exactly, no fuzziness needed.

**Step 2 — Fuzzy merge on the normalized column.** In Power Query: Home → Merge Queries → select the fuzzy match option. Set **Similarity threshold to 0.80**. Check **Ignore case**, **Ignore punctuation**, and **Combine text parts**. Set maximum matches to 1 initially.

**Step 3 — Add the corroborating signals.** After the merge, add:
- Exact amount match (flag if List A amount = List B amount)
- Date proximity (within 5 days)
- Invoice number or PO match if available

**Step 4 — Build a composite decision.** This is the part that answers your question.

| Name similarity | Amount match | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| ≥ 0.95 | Exact | Auto-accept, spot-check 5% |
| ≥ 0.95 | No match | Review — could be a duplicate or a partial |
| 0.85–0.94 | Exact | Review, but usually a match |
| 0.85–0.94 | No match | Manual review required |
| 0.70–0.84 | Exact | Review carefully — name is weak, amount carries it |
| 0.70–0.84 | No match | Likely no match; check for a genuine second vendor |
| < 0.70 | Any | No match. Manual lookup. |

**Step 5 — Track your false positive rate.** Once a month, sample 10 auto-accepted matches and verify them by hand. If more than one is wrong, tighten the threshold. This is how you calibrate rather than guess.

## How much manual review is reasonable

The answer depends on which error is worse. In reconciliation, **a false positive is worse than a false negative.** A missed match shows up as an unexplained difference you'll investigate. A wrong match hides a real difference and corrupts the rec.

So bias strict. Name-plus-amount at 0.85 is reasonable to accept. Name alone at 0.90 is not. And if you can't corroborate with a second field, review it — the review cost is minutes, the cost of a corrupted rec is a month-end scramble.

**The real long-term fix:** build a **crosswalk table.** Two columns — raw name (as it appears in each system) and canonical vendor ID. Once you've manually confirmed that "Acme Supply Co," "ACME SUPPLY," and "Acme Supply Company" are all vendor 1042, that mapping persists. Next month, you normalize through the crosswalk first, and you only fuzzy-match the genuinely new names. Within two or three cycles, you're fuzzy matching ten rows instead of a hundred, and your manual review burden drops to near zero.

Fuzzy matching is a stopgap. The crosswalk is the solution.

Can you suggest menu ideas for smaller dinner parties? Lately, my gatherings have been more intimate with just close friends and family, usually around a dozen people, so I’d love some inspiration for cozy meals that work well for this size.

At 12, something genuinely shifts: you can seat everyone at **one table** instead of running a buffet line, and you can serve one dish that's the star instead of a spread of options. That's what makes a dinner feel cozy rather than catered. Two 6-foot tables end to end seat 12 comfortably, and family-style passing is the whole point.

It's also October, which means braises, roasts, squash, apples, and — in your part of the world — mushrooms. Almost everything below leans that direction.

## 1. French bistro night (the make-ahead champion)

**Why it works at 12:** the entire meal is better made two days ahead. You do almost nothing on the day.

| Course | Dish | For 12 |
|---|---|---|
| Main | **Boeuf bourguignon** or **coq au vin** | 6 lbs chuck or 2 whole chickens cut up |
| Starch | Mashed potatoes or buttered egg noodles | 7 lbs potatoes |
| Veg | Buttered peas with pearl onions, or green beans with shallots | 3 lbs |
| Bread | Baguettes, warmed | 3 loaves |
| Dessert | **Apple galette** or a simple tarte tatin | 2 galettes |

**Make ahead:** braise 2 days out, refrigerate, reheat gently. It's better on day two. Make the galette dough ahead and bake day-of.

## 2. Sunday roast (impressive, mostly hands-off)

**Why it works at 12:** high impact, low attention. The oven does the work while you're with guests.

| Course | Dish | For 12 |
|---|---|---|
| Main | **Mustard-herb roast chicken** (2 birds) or **pork loin with apples** | 2 chickens, 4–5 lbs each |
| Starch | **Popovers** or roasted potatoes | 12 popovers |
| Veg | Roasted carrots and parsnips with thyme, or braised cabbage | 4 lbs |
| Salad | Simple green salad, lemon vinaigrette | 2 heads |
| Dessert | **Apple crumble** with vanilla ice cream | One 9x13 |

**Make ahead:** dry-brine the chicken the night before. Cut vegetables ahead. Crumble topping can be made days ahead and frozen.

## 3. Moroccan tagine night (one pot, scales perfectly)

**Why it works at 12:** a single pot, and it's forgiving — it can sit and wait.

| Course | Dish | For 12 |
|---|---|---|
| Main | **Lamb or chicken tagine** with apricots, olives, preserved lemon | 6 lbs |
| Starch | **Couscous** with butter and herbs | 4 cups dry |
| Veg | Roasted carrots with cumin and lemon; or harissa-roasted squash | 4 lbs |
| Condiment | Harissa yogurt, cilantro, toasted almonds | 2 cups |
| Dessert | **Orange-almond cake** or fresh dates with mint tea | One 9x13 |

**Make ahead:** tagine is better the next day. Couscous takes five minutes. This is the easiest menu on the list to execute.

## 4. Mushroom-forward fall supper (very Humboldt)

**Why it works at 12:** it's October, and you're near excellent local mushrooms. This is the menu that tastes like the season where you live.

| Course | Dish | For 12 |
|---|---|---|
| Starter | **Wild mushroom toast** on good bread with ricotta and thyme | 12 pieces |
| Main | **Mushroom and barley risotto**, or a **mushroom pot pie** | 3 cups dry barley or 2 large pies |
| Veg | Roasted delicata squash with sage brown butter | 3 squash |
| Salad | Arugula with shaved parmesan and lemon | 8 oz |
| Dessert | **Roasted pears with mascarpone and honey** | 12 halves |

**Make ahead:** pot pie assembles and freezes. Roast the squash ahead and warm it. The toast is a five-minute starter assembled to order at the table.

**One caution:** if you're using mushrooms you or a guest foraged, be certain of the identification. Store-bought is the safe call for a dinner party. If anyone is a forager, a small tasting plate is a lovely touch — but never the main.

## 5. Chicken pot pie night (pure comfort)

**Why it works at 12:** everyone loves it, it's inexpensive, and it's completely do-ahead.

| Course | Dish | For 12 |
|---|---|---|
| Main | **Chicken pot pie** in two 9x13 pans, or **cottage pie** | 4 lbs chicken or 5 lbs beef |
| Salad | Simple green salad, mustard vinaigrette | 2 heads |
| Veg | Roasted broccoli or green beans | 3 lbs |
| Dessert | **Chocolate pot de crème** made in small jars | 12 jars |

**Make ahead:** assemble the pies two days out, refrigerate unbaked, bake the day of. Pot de crème is a two-day dessert — make it the night before.

## 6. Curry night (feeds a crowd, reheats beautifully)

**Why it works at 12:** curry is better after it sits, it's cheap, and the sides are all make-ahead.

| Course | Dish | For 12 |
|---|---|---|
| Main | **Butter chicken** and/or **red lentil dal** | 5 lbs chicken + 2 lbs lentils |
| Starch | Basmati rice, cilantro, lemon | 4 cups dry |
| Bread | Naan, warmed in foil | 16 pieces |
| Sides | Cucumber raita, mango chutney, sliced red onion | 3 cups raita |
| Dessert | **Mango lassi** or rice pudding with cardamom | 12 servings |

**Make ahead:** both curries 2 days ahead. Rice in a rice cooker at the last minute.

## Quantities for 12, at a glance

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Meat for a braise | 5–6 lbs |
| Whole chicken | 2 birds, 4–5 lbs each |
| Starch (dry) | 3–4 cups rice, barley, or polenta |
| Mashed potatoes | 6–7 lbs |
| Vegetables | 3–4 lbs |
| Salad | 2 heads or 8 oz greens |
| Bread | 2–3 loaves |
| Dessert | One 9x13 or 12 individual servings |

## The one-table advantage

- **Serve family-style in the middle.** Passing dishes is what makes 12 feel intimate.
- **One star dish, two sides, one dessert.** At 12 you don't need a spread — you need a meal.
- **Don't assign seats, but do split couples.**
- **Put the bread and water on the table** so people aren't getting up mid-meal.
- **Light candles.** It's the cheapest thing you can do to make a dinner feel like an occasion.

## The common thread

Every menu above shares three properties: **one thing is the star, most of it is make-ahead, and it's better warm than hot.** That last one matters at 12, because something will sit for fifteen minutes while people arrive and settle. Braises, roasts, and curries all improve in that window. Delicate fish and risotto made to order don't.

Boeuf bourguignon is the right call — it's genuinely better on day two or three, which means the work is front-loaded and the day of the party is mostly reheating. Here's the full package.

## Quantities for 12

**Boeuf bourguignon**
| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Beef chuck, cut into 1½–2" cubes | 6 lbs |
| Bacon or lardons | 1 lb |
| Carrots, thick coins | 2 lbs |
| Yellow onions, diced | 3 large |
| Garlic | 6 cloves |
| Tomato paste | 4 tbsp |
| All-purpose flour | ½ cup |
| Red wine | 2 bottles (750 ml each) |
| Beef broth | 4 cups |
| Cremini mushrooms, quartered | 2 lbs |
| Frozen pearl onions | 1 lb |
| Butter | 4 tbsp |
| Olive oil | 3 tbsp |
| Thyme, bay leaves, salt, pepper | to taste |

**Mashed potatoes**
- 7 lbs Yukon Gold
- 3 sticks butter
- 2 cups whole milk or cream

**Peas and pearl onions**
- 3 lbs frozen peas
- 4 tbsp butter
- Optional: 2 shallots, minced

**Bread**
- 3 baguettes

**Apple galette (2 galettes)**
- 2½ cups flour
- 2 sticks cold butter
- 1 tsp salt, 2 tsp sugar
- ~½ cup ice water
- 12–14 apples (mix Granny Smith and Honeycrisp)
- 2 lemons
- ½ cup sugar, 2 tsp cinnamon
- 4 tbsp butter
- Apricot jam for glazing
- Vanilla ice cream to serve

## Shopping list by section

**Meat counter**
- 6 lbs beef chuck, cubed
- 1 lb bacon or lardons

**Produce**
- 2 lbs carrots
- 3 large yellow onions
- 1 head garlic
- 2 lbs cremini mushrooms
- 7 lbs Yukon Gold potatoes
- 12–14 apples
- 2 lemons
- 2 shallots (optional)
- Fresh thyme

**Frozen**
- 3 lbs peas
- 1 lb pearl onions

**Dairy**
- 5 sticks butter (you'll use about 4½)
- 2 cups whole milk or cream
- Vanilla ice cream

**Pantry**
- Tomato paste
- All-purpose flour (~6 cups total, for the braise and the galette)
- Beef broth (2 × 32 oz cartons)
- Bay leaves
- Cinnamon
- Apricot jam
- Olive oil

**Bakery**
- 3 baguettes

**Wine**
- 4–5 bottles (see pairings below)

**One equipment flag:** 6 lbs of beef plus liquid will not fit in a standard 6-quart Dutch oven. You need either a 9–10 quart Dutch oven, two pots, or a large roasting pan with a lid. Check before you shop — this is the thing that ruins the plan.

## Two-day timeline

### Day -2 (two days before)

**Morning or early afternoon**
- Shop. Buy the wine today so you're not doing it the day of.
- Cut the beef into 1½–2" cubes. Pat dry with paper towels and refrigerate. Dry beef browns; wet beef steams.
- Make both batches of galette dough: flour, salt, sugar, then cut in cold butter until pea-sized, add ice water until it just holds. Form two discs, wrap, refrigerate.

**Evening (allow 4 hours, mostly hands-off)**
- 5:00 — Take beef out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking.
- 5:30 — Cook the bacon in your largest pot until crisp. Remove, leave the fat.
- 5:45 — Brown the beef in batches. This is the long part, roughly 45 minutes for 6 lbs. Don't crowd the pot and don't rush it. Deep brown on all sides. Set aside with the bacon.
- 6:30 — Sauté onions and carrots in the same pot, 8 minutes. Add garlic, 1 minute. Add tomato paste, cook 2 minutes.
- 6:45 — Sprinkle flour over the vegetables, stir, cook 2 minutes.
- 6:50 — Pour in the wine. Scrape the bottom of the pot hard. Add broth, thyme, bay leaves, the beef, and the bacon. Bring to a simmer.
- 7:00 — Cover and move to a 325°F oven for 2½–3 hours, until the beef is fork-tender.
- 10:00 — Cool to room temperature, then refrigerate the whole pot, covered. **Do not skim the fat yet.** It solidifies overnight and lifts off in one piece.

### Day -1 (the day before)

**Morning (15 minutes)**
- Lift the solidified fat off the braise and discard. Taste and adjust salt.

**Afternoon (45 minutes)**
- Sauté the mushrooms in butter over high heat until browned and their liquid has cooked off. Set aside.
- Sauté the pearl onions in butter until lightly browned. Set aside. (Or use frozen and just warm them.)
- Refrigerate both separately. **Keep them separate from the braise** — if they sit in the sauce overnight they go soft.
- Peel the potatoes, cut into chunks, and store submerged in cold water in the fridge.
- Set the table. Do it today, not tomorrow.

**Evening**
- Chill the wine. Move the ice cream to the freezer if you bought it soft.

### Day of

| Time before guests | Task |
|---|---|
| 4 hrs | Take the braise out of the fridge. Let it come toward room temperature. |
| 3 hrs | Reheat the braise gently — low stovetop or 300°F oven. Don't boil it; boiling toughens the beef. Stir occasionally. |
| 2 hrs | Assemble and bake galette #1. Roll the dough, pile the sliced apples in the center, fold the edges over, dot with butter, brush with egg wash. Bake at 400°F for 35–40 minutes. |
| 1 hr | Start the potatoes. Boil until tender, then mash with butter, milk, salt. Hold warm with a lid. |
| 40 min | Assemble and bake galette #2, or hold it and bake during dinner for a warm-from-the-oven moment. |
| 20 min | Fold the mushrooms and pearl onions into the braise. Warm the bread in foil. |
| 10 min | Cook the peas with butter and shallots. |
| 0 | Serve. Family-style in the middle of the table. |

**If the braise is too thin:** simmer uncovered for 15 minutes.
**If it's too thick:** add a splash of broth or water.
**If it tastes flat:** a tablespoon of red wine vinegar or a squeeze of lemon. This is the most common fix and it works almost every time.

## Wine pairings, kept simple

**The main wine: Pinot Noir.** This is the classic pairing, and it's the same grape the dish is made from, so there's no wrong answer here.

- **If you want to spend more:** a real Bourgogne Rouge or a village-level Burgundy.
- **If you want value:** an Oregon Pinot Noir (Willamette Valley) or a California Pinot Noir (Sonoma Coast). Both are usually better than cheap Burgundy at the same price.
- **The practical move:** buy **two bottles of the same affordable Pinot Noir** — one for the pot, one for the table. You'll notice the difference, and it takes the guesswork out of the cooking wine question.

**A second red, if you want variety: Côtes du Rhône.** Grenache-Syrah blend, usually cheaper than Pinot, and it stands up beautifully to beef. Good to have as a backup bottle.

**For people who don't drink red:**
- **Crémant de Bourgogne** — French sparkling, affordable, festive, and a great aperitif while people arrive
- **White Burgundy (Chardonnay)** or a Sauvignon Blanc

**With the galette:**
- **Riesling** (German or Alsatian, off-dry) — the classic pairing with apple desserts
- Or **tawny port**, if you want to end on something richer
- Or just good coffee

**How much:** for 12 people, plan **4–5 bottles of red total**, plus a sparkling for arrival and one dessert wine. That's roughly 1½ glasses of red per person, which is a reasonable estimate if not everyone drinks heavily.

**Serving temperature:** reds at cellar temperature, not room temperature. Pop the red in the fridge for 20 minutes before serving — a slightly cool Pinot tastes much better than a warm one.

## Rough cost

| Category | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Beef and bacon | $45–65 |
| Wine (cooking + table) | $60–100 |
| Produce | $30–40 |
| Dairy | $15–20 |
| Pantry | $15 |
| Bread | $12 |
| Galette ingredients | $25 |
| **Total** | **$200–275, or about $17–23 per person** |

If you ask two or three guests to bring a salad or a cheese plate for before dinner, you can trim $30–40 and give yourself room on the wine.

## The one thing to remember

The garnish goes in **at the very end**, not overnight. Mushrooms and pearl onions that sit in the sauce for three days turn to mush. Keep them separate, fold them in twenty minutes before serving, and the dish tastes like you made it that afternoon.
